[Count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")**Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy**[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-1) ([/ˈ t oʊ l s t ɔɪ,ˈ t ɒ l-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-2)Russian: Лев Николаевич Толстой,[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-3)IPA:[[ˈlʲef nʲɪkɐˈla(j)ɪvʲɪtɕ tɐlˈstoj]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9e/Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg/Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg "File:Ru-Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy.ogg"); 9 September [[O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style") 28 August] 1828 – 20 November [[O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style") 7 November] 1910),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) usually referred to in English as **Leo Tolstoy**, was a Russian writer. He is regarded as one of the greatest and most influential authors of all time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Burt-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Popova-6)

Born to an aristocratic family, Tolstoy achieved acclaim in his twenties with his semi-autobiographical trilogy, _[Childhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)")_, _[Boyhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyhood\_(novel) "Boyhood (novel)")_ and _[Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Youth (Tolstoy novel)")_ (1852–1856), and with _[Sevastopol Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol\_Sketches "Sevastopol Sketches")_ (1855), based on his experiences in the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War"). _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ (1869), _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina "Anna Karenina")_ (1878), and _[Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Resurrection (Tolstoy novel)")_ (1899), which is based on his "youthful sins",[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-7) are often cited as pinnacles of [realist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism "Literary realism") fiction[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) and three of the greatest novels ever written.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Burt-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Popova-6) His _oeuvre_ includes short stories such as "[Alyosha the Pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alyosha_the_Pot "Alyosha the Pot")" (1911) and "[After the Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_the_Ball_(short_story) "After the Ball (short story)")" (1911) and [novellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novella "Novella") such as _[Family Happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family\_Happiness "Family Happiness")_ (1859), _[The Death of Ivan Ilyich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_of\_Ivan\_Ilyich "The Death of Ivan Ilyich")_ (1886), _[The Kreutzer Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kreutzer\_Sonata "The Kreutzer Sonata")_ (1889), _[The Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Devil\_(novella) "The Devil (novella)")_ (1911), and _[Hadji Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadji\_Murat\_(novella) "Hadji Murat (novella)")_ (1912). He also wrote [plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theater) "Play (theater)") and essays concerning philosophical, moral and religious themes.

In the 1870s, Tolstoy experienced a profound moral crisis, followed by what he regarded as an equally profound spiritual awakening, as outlined in his non-fiction work _[Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession\_(Leo\_Tolstoy) "Confession (Leo Tolstoy)")_ (1882). His literal interpretation of the ethical teachings of Jesus, centering on the [Sermon on the Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon_on_the_Mount "Sermon on the Mount"), caused him to become a fervent [Christian anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_anarchist "Christian anarchist") and [pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifist "Pacifist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) His ideas on [nonviolent resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_resistance "Nonviolent resistance"), expressed in such works as _[The Kingdom of God Is Within You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kingdom\_of\_God\_Is\_Within\_You "The Kingdom of God Is Within You")_ (1894), had a profound impact on such pivotal 20th-century figures as [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-ResistNotEvil-8)Ludwig Wittgenstein,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-9)[Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-10) and [James Bevel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bevel "James Bevel").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-11) He also became a dedicated advocate of [Georgism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgism "Georgism"), the economic philosophy of [Henry George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_George "Henry George"), which he incorporated into his writing, particularly in _Resurrection_.

Tolstoy received praise from countless authors and critics, both during his lifetime and after. [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf "Virginia Woolf") called Tolstoy "the greatest of all novelists", and [Gary Saul Morson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Saul_Morson "Gary Saul Morson") referred to _War and Peace_ as the greatest of all novels. He received nominations for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") every year from 1902 to 1906 and for the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") in 1901, 1902, and 1909. Tolstoy never being awarded a Nobel Prize remains a major [Nobel Prize controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature_controversies "Nobel Prize in Literature controversies").

## Origins

Main article: [Tolstoy family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoy_family "Tolstoy family")

The [Tolstoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoy_family "Tolstoy family") were a well-known family of old [Russian nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_nobility "Russian nobility") who traced their ancestry to a mythical[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Barlett_2011_14-12) nobleman named Indris described by [Pyotr Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Andreyevich_Tolstoy "Pyotr Andreyevich Tolstoy") as arriving "from Nemec, from the lands of Caesar" to [Chernigov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernigov "Chernigov") in 1353 along with his two sons Litvinos (or Litvonis) and Zimonten (or Zigmont) and a [druzhina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druzhina "Druzhina") of 3000 people.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-bunin-14) Indris was then converted to [Eastern Orthodoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church"), under the name of Leonty, and his sons as Konstantin and Feodor. Konstantin's grandson Andrei Kharitonovich was nicknamed Tolstiy (translated as _fat_) by [Vasily II of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_II_of_Moscow "Vasily II of Moscow") after he moved from Chernigov to Moscow.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-bunin-14)

Because of the pagan names and the fact that Chernigov at the time was ruled by [Demetrius I Starshy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demetrius_I_Starshy "Demetrius I Starshy"), some researchers concluded that they were [Lithuanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanians "Lithuanians") who arrived from the [Grand Duchy of Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania "Grand Duchy of Lithuania").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-16) At the same time, no mention of Indris was ever found in the 14th-to-16th-century documents, while the [Chernigov Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Russian_Chronicles "Old Russian Chronicles") used by Pyotr Tolstoy as a reference were lost.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13) The first documented members of the Tolstoy family also lived during the 17th century, thus Pyotr Tolstoy himself is generally considered the founder of the noble house, being granted the title of [count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count") by [Peter the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great "Peter the Great").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-18)

## Life and career

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_%284x5_cropped%29.jpg/250px-Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_%284x5_cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_(4x5_cropped).jpg)

Tolstoy at age 20, c.1848

Tolstoy was born at [Yasnaya Polyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasnaya_Polyana "Yasnaya Polyana"), a family estate 12 kilometres (7.5 mi) southwest of [Tula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tula,_Russia "Tula, Russia"), and 200 kilometres (120 mi) south of Moscow. He was the fourth of five children of [Count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")[Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Ilyich_Tolstoy "Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy") (1794–1837), a veteran of the [Patriotic War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia "French invasion of Russia"), and Princess Mariya Tolstaya (née [Volkonskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkonsky "Volkonsky"); 1790–1830). His mother died when he was two and his father when he was nine.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) Tolstoy and his siblings were brought up by relatives.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) In 1844, he began studying law and oriental languages at [Kazan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazan_University "Kazan University"), where teachers described him as "both unable and unwilling to learn".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) Tolstoy left the university in the middle of his studies,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) returned to Yasnaya Polyana and then spent much time in Moscow, Tula and Saint Petersburg, leading a lax and leisurely lifestyle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) He began writing during this period,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) including his first novel _[Childhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)")_, a fictitious account of his own youth, which was published in 1852.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) In 1851, after running up heavy gambling debts, he went with his older brother to the [Caucasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus_(geographic_region) "Caucasus (geographic region)") and joined the [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Russian_Army "Imperial Russian Army"). Tolstoy served as a young artillery officer during the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War") and was in Sevastopol during the 11-month-long [siege of Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sevastopol_(1854%E2%80%9355) "Siege of Sevastopol (1854–55)") in 1854–55,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-BBCTen-20) including the [Battle of the Chernaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Chernaya "Battle of the Chernaya"). During the war he was recognised for his courage and promoted to lieutenant.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-BBCTen-20) He was appalled by the number of deaths involved in warfare,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) and left the army after the end of the Crimean War.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4)

His experience in the army, and two trips around Europe in 1857 and 1860–61 converted Tolstoy from a dissolute and privileged society author to a non-violent and spiritual [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism"). Others who followed the same path were [Alexander Herzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Herzen "Alexander Herzen"), [Mikhail Bakunin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Bakunin "Mikhail Bakunin") and [Peter Kropotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kropotkin "Peter Kropotkin"). During his 1857 visit, Tolstoy witnessed a public execution in Paris, a traumatic experience that marked the rest of his life. In a letter to his friend [Vasily Botkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Botkin "Vasily Botkin"), Tolstoy wrote: "The truth is that the State is a conspiracy designed not only to exploit, but above all to corrupt its citizens ... Henceforth, I shall never serve any government anywhere."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-21) Tolstoy's concept of [non-violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-violence "Non-violence") or [ahimsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa "Ahimsa") was bolstered when he read a [German version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirukkural_translations_into_German "Tirukkural translations into German") of the [Tirukkural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirukkural "Tirukkural").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-PearlsOfInsp_Rajaram-22)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Walsh2018-23) He later instilled the concept in [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") through his "_[A Letter to a Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Letter\_to\_a\_Hindu "A Letter to a Hindu")_" when young Gandhi corresponded with him seeking his advice.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Walsh2018-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-gandhi-25)

His European trip in 1860–61 shaped both his political and literary development when he met [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo"). Tolstoy read Hugo's newly finished _[Les Misérables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Mis%C3%A9rables "Les Misérables")_. The similar evocation of battle scenes in Hugo's novel and Tolstoy's _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ indicates this influence. Tolstoy's political philosophy was also influenced by a March 1861 visit to French anarchist [Pierre-Joseph Proudhon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Joseph_Proudhon "Pierre-Joseph Proudhon"), then living in exile under an assumed name in Brussels. Tolstoy reviewed Proudhon's forthcoming publication, _La Guerre et la Paix_ ("_War and Peace_" in French), and later used the title for his masterpiece. The two men also discussed education, as Tolstoy wrote in his educational notebooks: "If I recount this conversation with Proudhon, it is to show that, in my personal experience, he was the only man who understood the significance of education and of the printing press in our time."

Fired by enthusiasm, Tolstoy returned to Yasnaya Polyana and founded 13 schools for the children of Russia's peasants, who had just been [emancipated from serfdom in 1861](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_reform_of_1861 "Emancipation reform of 1861"). Tolstoy described the schools' principles in his 1862 essay "The School at Yasnaya Polyana".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-26) His educational experiments were short-lived, partly due to harassment by the [Tsarist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") secret police. However, as a direct forerunner to [A.S. Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.S._Neill "A.S. Neill")'s [Summerhill School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summerhill_School "Summerhill School"), the school at Yasnaya Polyana[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-27) can justifiably be claimed the first example of a coherent theory of [democratic education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_education "Democratic education").

## Personal life

The death of his brother Nikolay in 1860 had an impact on Tolstoy, and led him to a desire to marry.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) On 23 September 1862, Tolstoy married [Sophia Andreevna Behrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Tolstaya "Sophia Tolstaya"), who was sixteen years his junior and the daughter of a court physician. She was called Sonya, the Russian diminutive of Sofia, by her family and friends.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28) They had 13 children, eight of whom survived childhood:[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-29)

Tolstoy's wife [Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Tolstaya "Sophia Tolstaya") and their daughter [Alexandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Tolstaya "Alexandra Tolstaya")

*   [Count Sergei Lvovich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Tolstoy "Sergei Tolstoy") (1863–1947), composer and ethnomusicologist
*   [Countess Tatyana Lvovna Tolstaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatyana_Sukhotina-Tolstaya "Tatyana Sukhotina-Tolstaya") (1864–1950), wife of Mikhail Sergeevich Sukhotin
*   [Count Ilya Lvovich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Tolstoy "Ilya Tolstoy") (1866–1933), writer
*   [Count Lev Lvovich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev_Lvovich_Tolstoy "Lev Lvovich Tolstoy") (1869–1945), writer and sculptor
*   Countess Maria Lvovna Tolstaya (1871–1906), wife of [Nikolai Leonidovich Obolensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Leonidovich_Obolensky "Nikolai Leonidovich Obolensky")
*   Count Peter Lvovich Tolstoy (1872–1873), died in infancy
*   Count Nikolai Lvovich Tolstoy (1874–1875), died in infancy
*   Countess Varvara Lvovna Tolstaya (1875–1875), died in infancy
*   Count Andrei Lvovich Tolstoy (1877–1916), served in the [Russo-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War")
*   Count Michael Lvovich Tolstoy (1879–1944)
*   Count Alexei Lvovich Tolstoy (1881–1886)
*   [Countess Alexandra Lvovna Tolstaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Tolstaya "Alexandra Tolstaya") (1884–1979)
*   Count Ivan Lvovich Tolstoy (1888–1895)

Tolstoy, on the eve of their marriage, gave her his diaries detailing his extensive sexual past and the fact that one of the serfs on his estate had borne him a son.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28) Even so, their early married life was happy and allowed Tolstoy much freedom and the support system to compose _War and Peace_ and _Anna Karenina_, with Sonya acting as his secretary, editor, and financial manager. Sonya was copying and hand-writing his epic works time after time. Tolstoy would continue editing _War and Peace_ and had to have clean final drafts to be delivered to the publisher.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-30)

However, their later life together has been described by [A.N. Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.N._Wilson "A.N. Wilson") as one of the unhappiest in literary history. Tolstoy's relationship with his wife deteriorated as his beliefs became increasingly radical. This saw him seeking to reject his inherited and earned wealth, including the renunciation of the copyrights on his earlier works.

When he was finishing up the last installments of _Anna Karenina_ Tolstoy was in an anguished state of mind and he began putting away guns and ropes out of fear that he would kill himself.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-31)

Some members of the Tolstoy family left Russia in the aftermath of the [1905 Russian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1905_Russian_Revolution "1905 Russian Revolution"), or after the establishment of the Soviet Union following the 1917 [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution"), and many of Leo Tolstoy's relatives and descendants today live in Sweden, Germany, the United Kingdom, France and the United States. Tolstoy's son, Count [Lev Lvovich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev_Lvovich_Tolstoy "Lev Lvovich Tolstoy"), settled in Sweden and married a Swedish woman, and their descendants with family names including Tolstoy, [Paus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paus_family "Paus family") and Ceder still live in Sweden. The Paus branch of the family is also closely related to [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-32) Leo Tolstoy's last surviving grandchild, Countess [Tatiana Tolstoy-Paus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatiana_Tolstoy-Paus "Tatiana Tolstoy-Paus"), died in 2007 at [Herresta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herresta "Herresta") manor in Sweden, which is owned by Tolstoy's descendants.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-33) Swedish writer Daria Paus and jazz singer [Viktoria Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktoria_Tolstoy "Viktoria Tolstoy") are among Leo Tolstoy's Swedish descendants.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-34)

One of his great-great-grandsons, Vladimir Tolstoy (born 1962), has been a director of the [Yasnaya Polyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasnaya_Polyana "Yasnaya Polyana") museum since 1994 and an adviser to the [President of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Russia "President of Russia") on cultural affairs since 2012.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-36)[Ilya Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Tolstoy "Ilya Tolstoy")'s great-grandson, [Pyotr Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Olegovich_Tolstoy "Pyotr Olegovich Tolstoy"), is a well-known Russian journalist and TV presenter as well as a [State Duma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_State_Duma "7th State Duma") deputy since 2016. His cousin [Fyokla Tolstaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyokla_Tolstaya "Fyokla Tolstaya") (born Anna Tolstaya in 1971), daughter of the acclaimed Soviet [Slavist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavist "Slavist") Nikita Tolstoy ([ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%BE%D0%BB%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B9,%20%D0%9D%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B8%D1%82%D0%B0%20%D0%98%D0%BB%D1%8C%D0%B8%D1%87 "ru:Толстой, Никита Ильич")) (1923–1996), is also a Russian journalist, TV and radio host.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-37) American actress [Pati Behrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pati_Behrs "Pati Behrs") (1922–2004) was his wife's great-niece and her daughter, screenwriter [Sean Catherine Derek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Catherine_Derek "Sean Catherine Derek") (b. 1953), is her great-grandniece.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-38)

## Novels and fictional works

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy%2C_1873.jpg/250px-Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy%2C_1873.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy,_1873.jpg)

Portrait of Leo Tolstoy by [Ivan Kramskoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Kramskoi "Ivan Kramskoi"), 1873

Tolstoy is considered one of the giants of Russian literature; his works include the novels _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ and _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina "Anna Karenina")_ and novellas such as _[Hadji Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadji\_Murat\_(novella) "Hadji Murat (novella)")_ and _[The Death of Ivan Ilyich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_of\_Ivan\_Ilyich "The Death of Ivan Ilyich")_. Tolstoy's earliest works, the autobiographical novels [_Childhood_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood_(Tolstoy_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)"), [_Boyhood_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyhood_(novel) "Boyhood (novel)"), and [_Youth_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_(Tolstoy_novel) "Youth (Tolstoy novel)") (1852–1856), tell of a rich landowner's son and his slow realization of the chasm between himself and his peasants. Though he later rejected them as sentimental, a great deal of Tolstoy's own life is revealed. They retain their relevance as accounts of the universal story of growing up. Tolstoy served as a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podporuchik "Podporuchik") in an artillery regiment during the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War"), recounted in his _[Sevastopol Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol\_Sketches "Sevastopol Sketches")_. His experiences in battle helped stir his subsequent pacifism and gave him material for realistic depiction of the horrors of war in his later work.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-39)

His fiction consistently attempts to convey realistically the Russian society in which he lived.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-40)_[The Cossacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cossacks\_(novel) "The Cossacks (novel)")_ (1863) describes the [Cossack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack") life and people through a story of a Russian aristocrat in love with a Cossack girl. _Anna Karenina_ (1877) tells parallel stories of an adulterous woman trapped by the conventions and falsities of society and of a philosophical landowner (much like Tolstoy), who works alongside the peasants in the fields and seeks to reform their lives. Tolstoy not only drew from his own life experiences but also created characters in his own image, such as Pierre Bezukhov and Prince Andrei in _War and Peace_, Levin in _Anna Karenina_ and to some extent, Prince Nekhlyudov in _Resurrection_. [Richard Pevear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Pevear_and_Larissa_Volokhonsky "Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky"), who translated many of Tolstoy's works, said of Tolstoy's signature style, "His works are full of provocation and irony, and written with broad and elaborately developed rhetorical devices."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-41)

_War and Peace_ is generally thought to be one of the greatest novels ever written, remarkable for its dramatic breadth and unity. Its vast canvas includes 580 characters, many historical with others fictional. The story moves from family life to the headquarters of [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_I_of_France "Napoleon I of France"), from the court of [Alexander I of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Russia "Alexander I of Russia") to the battlefields of [Austerlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Austerlitz "Battle of Austerlitz") and [Borodino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Borodino "Battle of Borodino"). Tolstoy's original idea for the novel was to investigate the causes of the [Decembrist revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decembrist_revolt "Decembrist revolt"), to which it refers only in the last chapters, from which can be deduced that [Andrei Bolkonsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Nikolayevich_Bolkonsky "Andrei Nikolayevich Bolkonsky")'s son will become one of the Decembrists. The novel explores Tolstoy's theory of history, and in particular the insignificance of individuals such as Napoleon and Alexander. Somewhat surprisingly, Tolstoy did not consider _War and Peace_ to be a novel (nor did he consider many of the great Russian fictions written at that time to be novels). This view becomes less surprising if one considers that Tolstoy was a novelist of the [realist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_(arts) "Realism (arts)") school who considered the novel to be a framework for the examination of social and political issues in nineteenth-century life.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-42)_War and Peace_ (which is to Tolstoy really an [epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") in prose) therefore did not qualify. Tolstoy called _Anna Karenina_ his first novel.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-43)

After _Anna Karenina_, Tolstoy concentrated on Christian themes, and his later novels such as _The Death of Ivan Ilyich_ (1886) and _[What Is to Be Done?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What\_Is\_to\_Be\_Done%3F\_(Tolstoy) "What Is to Be Done? (Tolstoy)")_ develop a radical [anarcho-pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarcho-pacifist "Anarcho-pacifist") Christian philosophy which led to his excommunication from the [Russian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church "Russian Orthodox Church") in 1901.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-44) After his religious conversion, Tolstoy came to reject most modern Western culture, including his novels _War and Peace_ and _Anna Karenina_, as elitist "counterfeit art" with different aims from the Christian art of universal brotherly love he sought to express.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBartlett2011369-45)

In his novel _[Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Resurrection (Tolstoy novel)")_, Tolstoy attempts to expose the injustice of man-made laws and the hypocrisy of an institutionalized church. Tolstoy also explores and explains the economic philosophy of [Georgism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgism "Georgism"), of which he had become a very strong advocate towards the end of his life.

Tolstoy also tried writing poetry, with several soldier songs written during his military service, and fairy tales in verse such as _Volga-bogatyr_ and _Oaf_ stylized as national folk songs. They were written between 1871 and 1874 for his _Russian Book for Reading_, a collection of short stories in four volumes (total of 629 stories in various genres) published along with the _New Azbuka_ textbook and addressed to schoolchildren. Nevertheless, he was skeptical about poetry as a genre. As he famously said, "Writing poetry is like ploughing and dancing at the same time." According to [Valentin Bulgakov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Bulgakov "Valentin Bulgakov"), he criticised poets, including [Alexander Pushkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pushkin "Alexander Pushkin"), for their "false" epithets used "simply to make it rhyme".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-47)

## Critical appraisal by other authors

Tolstoy's contemporaries paid him lofty tributes. [Fyodor Dostoyevsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Dostoyevsky "Fyodor Dostoyevsky"), who died thirty years before Tolstoy, admired and was delighted by Tolstoy's novels (and, conversely, Tolstoy also admired Dostoyevsky's work).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Dosteoevsky-48)[Gustave Flaubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Flaubert "Gustave Flaubert"), on reading a translation of _War and Peace_, exclaimed, "What an artist and what a psychologist!" [Anton Chekhov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Chekhov "Anton Chekhov"), who often visited Tolstoy at his country estate, wrote, "When literature possesses a Tolstoy, it is easy and pleasant to be a writer; even when you know you have achieved nothing yourself and are still achieving nothing, this is not as terrible as it might otherwise be, because Tolstoy achieves for everyone. What he does serves to justify all the hopes and aspirations invested in literature." The 19th-century British poet and critic [Matthew Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Arnold "Matthew Arnold") wrote that "A novel by Tolstoy is not a work of art but a piece of life."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4)[Isaac Babel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Babel "Isaac Babel") said that "if the world could write by itself, it would write like Tolstoy."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4)

Later novelists continued to appreciate Tolstoy's art, but sometimes also expressed criticism. [Arthur Conan Doyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Conan_Doyle "Arthur Conan Doyle") wrote, "I am attracted by his earnestness and by his power of detail, but I am repelled by his looseness of construction and by his unreasonable and impracticable mysticism."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-ACD-49)[Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf "Virginia Woolf") declared him "the greatest of all novelists".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Tolstoy-2023-50)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4)[James Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce") noted that, "He is never dull, never stupid, never tired, never pedantic, never theatrical!" [Thomas Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann") wrote of Tolstoy's seemingly guileless artistry: "Seldom did art work so much like nature." [Vladimir Nabokov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Nabokov "Vladimir Nabokov") heaped superlatives upon _[The Death of Ivan Ilyich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_of\_Ivan\_Ilyich "The Death of Ivan Ilyich")_ and _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina "Anna Karenina")_; he questioned, however, the reputation of _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ and sharply criticized _[Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Resurrection (Tolstoy novel)")_ and _[The Kreutzer Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kreutzer\_Sonata "The Kreutzer Sonata")_. However, Nabokov called Tolstoy the "greatest Russian writer of prose fiction".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-51) Critic [Harold Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Bloom "Harold Bloom") called _[Hadji Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadji\_Murat\_(novella) "Hadji Murat (novella)")_ "my personal touchstone for the sublime in prose fiction, to me the best story in the world."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-52) When [William Faulkner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Faulkner "William Faulkner") was asked to list what he thought were the three greatest novels, he replied: "_Anna Karenina, Anna Karenina_, and _Anna Karenina_".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Tolstoy-2023-50) Critic [Gary Saul Morson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Saul_Morson "Gary Saul Morson") referred to _War and Peace_ as the greatest of all novels.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Morson-53)

## Ethical, political and religious beliefs

### Schopenhauer

After reading [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schopenhauer "Arthur Schopenhauer")'s _[The World as Will and Representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_World\_as\_Will\_and\_Representation "The World as Will and Representation")_, Tolstoy gradually became converted to the ascetic morality upheld in that work as the proper spiritual path for the upper classes. In 1869 he writes: "Do you know what this summer has meant for me? Constant raptures over Schopenhauer and a whole series of spiritual delights which I've never experienced before....no student has ever studied so much on his course, and learned so much, as I have this summer."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-54)

In Chapter VI of _[Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession\_(Leo\_Tolstoy) "Confession (Leo Tolstoy)")_, Tolstoy quoted the final paragraph of Schopenhauer's work. It explains how a complete [denial of self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-denial "Self-denial") causes only a relative nothingness which is not to be feared. Tolstoy was struck by the description of Christian, Buddhist, and Hindu ascetic renunciation as being the path to holiness. After reading passages such as the following, which abound in Schopenhauer's ethical chapters, the Russian nobleman chose poverty and formal denial of the will:

> But this very necessity of involuntary suffering (by poor people) for [eternal salvation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternal_salvation "Eternal salvation") is also expressed by that utterance of the Savior ([Matthew 19:24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_19:24 "Matthew 19:24")): "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." Therefore, those who were greatly in earnest about their eternal salvation, chose [voluntary poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_living "Simple living") when fate had denied this to them and they had been born in wealth. Thus Buddha [Sakyamuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakyamuni "Sakyamuni") was born a prince, but voluntarily took to the mendicant's staff; and [Francis of Assisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi "Francis of Assisi"), the founder of the [mendicant orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendicant_orders "Mendicant orders") who, as a youngster at a ball, where the daughters of all the notabilities were sitting together, was asked: "Now Francis, will you not soon make your choice from these beauties?" and who replied: "I have made a far more beautiful choice!" "Whom?" "_La povertà_ (poverty)": whereupon he abandoned every thing shortly afterwards and wandered through the land as a mendicant.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-55)

### Christianity

In 1884, Tolstoy wrote a book called _What I Believe_, in which he openly confessed his Christian beliefs. He affirmed his belief in Jesus Christ's teachings and was particularly influenced by the [Sermon on the Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon_on_the_Mount "Sermon on the Mount"), and the injunction to [turn the other cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_the_other_cheek "Turn the other cheek"), which he understood as a "commandment of non-resistance to evil by force" and a doctrine of [pacifism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifism "Pacifism") and [nonviolence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence "Nonviolence"). In his work _The Kingdom of God Is Within You_, he explains that he considered mistaken the Church's doctrine because they had made a "perversion" of Christ's teachings. Tolstoy also received letters from American [Quakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers") who introduced him to the non-violence writings of Quaker Christians such as [George Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Fox "George Fox"), [William Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn "William Penn"), and [Jonathan Dymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Dymond "Jonathan Dymond"). Later, various versions of "Tolstoy's Bible" were published, indicating the passages Tolstoy most relied on, specifically, the reported words of Jesus himself.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-56)

[Mohandas K. Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohandas_Karamchand_Gandhi "Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi") and other residents of [Tolstoy Farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoy_Farm "Tolstoy Farm"), South Africa, 1910

Tolstoy believed that a true Christian could find lasting happiness by striving for inner perfection through following the [Great Commandment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commandment "Great Commandment") of loving one's neighbor and God, rather than guidance from the Church or state. Another distinct attribute of his philosophy based on Christ's teachings is [nonresistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonresistance "Nonresistance") during conflict. This idea, communicated in Tolstoy's book _[The Kingdom of God Is Within You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kingdom\_of\_God\_Is\_Within\_You "The Kingdom of God Is Within You")_, directly influenced [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") and by extension nonviolent resistance movements as a whole.

Tolstoy believed that the aristocracy was a burden on the poor.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-57) He opposed [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_property "Private property") land ownership and the institution of marriage, and valued chastity and sexual abstinence (discussed in _[Father Sergius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father\_Sergius "Father Sergius")_ and his preface to _The Kreutzer Sonata_), ideals also held by the young Gandhi. Tolstoy's passion from the depth of his austere moral views is reflected in his later work.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-58) One example is the sequence of the temptation of Sergius in _Father Sergius_. [Maxim Gorky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_Gorky "Maxim Gorky") relates how Tolstoy once read this passage before him and Chekhov, and Tolstoy was moved to tears by the end of the reading. Later passages of rare power include the personal crises faced by the protagonists of _The Death of Ivan Ilyich_, and of _[Master and Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master\_and\_Man\_(short\_story) "Master and Man (short story)")_, where the main character in the former and the reader in the latter are made aware of the foolishness of the protagonists' lives.

In 1886, Tolstoy wrote to the Russian [explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Russian_explorers "List of Russian explorers") and anthropologist [Nicholas Miklouho-Maclay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Miklouho-Maclay "Nicholas Miklouho-Maclay"), who was one of the first anthropologists to refute [polygenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygenism "Polygenism"), the view that the different [races of mankind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(human_categorization) "Race (human categorization)") belonged to different species: "You were the first to demonstrate beyond question by your experience that man is man everywhere, that is, a kind, sociable being with whom communication can and should be established through kindness and truth, not guns and spirits."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-59)

Tolstoy had a profound influence on the development of [Christian anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_anarchist "Christian anarchist") thought.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-60) Tolstoy believed being a Christian required him to be a pacifist; the apparently inevitable waging of war by governments is why he is considered a philosophical anarchist. The [Tolstoyans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoyan "Tolstoyan") were a small Christian anarchist group formed by Tolstoy's companion, [Vladimir Chertkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Chertkov "Vladimir Chertkov") (1854–1936), to spread Tolstoy's religious teachings. From 1892, he regularly met with the student-activist [Vasily Maklakov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Maklakov "Vasily Maklakov") who would defend several Tolstoyans; they discussed the fate of the [Doukhobors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doukhobors "Doukhobors"). Philosopher [Peter Kropotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kropotkin "Peter Kropotkin") wrote of Tolstoy in the article on anarchism in the _[1911 Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911\_Encyclop%C3%A6dia\_Britannica "1911 Encyclopædia Britannica")_:

> Without naming himself an anarchist, Leo Tolstoy, like his predecessors in the popular religious movements of the 15th and 16th centuries, [Chojecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petr_Chel%C4%8Dick%C3%BD "Petr Chelčický"), [Denk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Denck "Hans Denck") and many others, took the anarchist position as regards the [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(polity) "State (polity)") and [property rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_right "Property right"), deducing his conclusions from the general spirit of the teachings of Jesus and from the necessary dictates of reason.
> 
> 
> With all the might of his talent, Tolstoy made (especially in _The Kingdom of God Is Within You_) a powerful criticism of the church, the state and law altogether, and especially of the present [property laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_law "Property law"). He describes the state as the domination of the wicked ones, supported by brutal force. Robbers, he says, are far less dangerous than a well-organized government. He makes a searching criticism of the prejudices which are current now concerning the benefits conferred upon men by the church, the state, and the existing distribution of property, and from the teachings of Jesus he deduces the rule of nonresistance and the absolute condemnation of all wars.
> 
> 
> His religious arguments are, however, so well combined with arguments borrowed from a dispassionate observation of the present evils, that the anarchist portions of his works appeal to the religious and the non-religious reader alike.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-61)

[Count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")**Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy**[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-1) ([/ˈ t oʊ l s t ɔɪ,ˈ t ɒ l-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-2)Russian: Лев Николаевич Толстой,[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-3)IPA:[[ˈlʲef nʲɪkɐˈla(j)ɪvʲɪtɕ tɐlˈstoj]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9e/Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg/Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ru-Lev_Nikolayevich_Tolstoy.ogg "File:Ru-Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy.ogg"); 9 September [[O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style") 28 August] 1828 – 20 November [[O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style") 7 November] 1910),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) usually referred to in English as **Leo Tolstoy**, was a Russian writer. He is regarded as one of the greatest and most influential authors of all time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Burt-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Popova-6)

Born to an aristocratic family, Tolstoy achieved acclaim in his twenties with his semi-autobiographical trilogy, _[Childhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)")_, _[Boyhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyhood\_(novel) "Boyhood (novel)")_ and _[Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Youth (Tolstoy novel)")_ (1852–1856), and with _[Sevastopol Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol\_Sketches "Sevastopol Sketches")_ (1855), based on his experiences in the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War"). _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ (1869), _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina "Anna Karenina")_ (1878), and _[Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Resurrection (Tolstoy novel)")_ (1899), which is based on his "youthful sins",[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-7) are often cited as pinnacles of [realist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism "Literary realism") fiction[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) and three of the greatest novels ever written.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Burt-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Popova-6) His _oeuvre_ includes short stories such as "[Alyosha the Pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alyosha_the_Pot "Alyosha the Pot")" (1911) and "[After the Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_the_Ball_(short_story) "After the Ball (short story)")" (1911) and [novellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novella "Novella") such as _[Family Happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family\_Happiness "Family Happiness")_ (1859), _[The Death of Ivan Ilyich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_of\_Ivan\_Ilyich "The Death of Ivan Ilyich")_ (1886), _[The Kreutzer Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kreutzer\_Sonata "The Kreutzer Sonata")_ (1889), _[The Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Devil\_(novella) "The Devil (novella)")_ (1911), and _[Hadji Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadji\_Murat\_(novella) "Hadji Murat (novella)")_ (1912). He also wrote [plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theater) "Play (theater)") and essays concerning philosophical, moral and religious themes.

In the 1870s, Tolstoy experienced a profound moral crisis, followed by what he regarded as an equally profound spiritual awakening, as outlined in his non-fiction work _[Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession\_(Leo\_Tolstoy) "Confession (Leo Tolstoy)")_ (1882). His literal interpretation of the ethical teachings of Jesus, centering on the [Sermon on the Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon_on_the_Mount "Sermon on the Mount"), caused him to become a fervent [Christian anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_anarchist "Christian anarchist") and [pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifist "Pacifist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) His ideas on [nonviolent resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_resistance "Nonviolent resistance"), expressed in such works as _[The Kingdom of God Is Within You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kingdom\_of\_God\_Is\_Within\_You "The Kingdom of God Is Within You")_ (1894), had a profound impact on such pivotal 20th-century figures as [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-ResistNotEvil-8)Ludwig Wittgenstein,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-9)[Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-10) and [James Bevel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bevel "James Bevel").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-11) He also became a dedicated advocate of [Georgism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgism "Georgism"), the economic philosophy of [Henry George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_George "Henry George"), which he incorporated into his writing, particularly in _Resurrection_.

Tolstoy received praise from countless authors and critics, both during his lifetime and after. [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf "Virginia Woolf") called Tolstoy "the greatest of all novelists", and [Gary Saul Morson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Saul_Morson "Gary Saul Morson") referred to _War and Peace_ as the greatest of all novels. He received nominations for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") every year from 1902 to 1906 and for the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") in 1901, 1902, and 1909. Tolstoy never being awarded a Nobel Prize remains a major [Nobel Prize controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature_controversies "Nobel Prize in Literature controversies").

## Origins

Main article: [Tolstoy family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoy_family "Tolstoy family")

The [Tolstoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolstoy_family "Tolstoy family") were a well-known family of old [Russian nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_nobility "Russian nobility") who traced their ancestry to a mythical[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Barlett_2011_14-12) nobleman named Indris described by [Pyotr Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Andreyevich_Tolstoy "Pyotr Andreyevich Tolstoy") as arriving "from Nemec, from the lands of Caesar" to [Chernigov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernigov "Chernigov") in 1353 along with his two sons Litvinos (or Litvonis) and Zimonten (or Zigmont) and a [druzhina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druzhina "Druzhina") of 3000 people.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-bunin-14) Indris was then converted to [Eastern Orthodoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church"), under the name of Leonty, and his sons as Konstantin and Feodor. Konstantin's grandson Andrei Kharitonovich was nicknamed Tolstiy (translated as _fat_) by [Vasily II of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_II_of_Moscow "Vasily II of Moscow") after he moved from Chernigov to Moscow.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-bunin-14)

Because of the pagan names and the fact that Chernigov at the time was ruled by [Demetrius I Starshy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demetrius_I_Starshy "Demetrius I Starshy"), some researchers concluded that they were [Lithuanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanians "Lithuanians") who arrived from the [Grand Duchy of Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania "Grand Duchy of Lithuania").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-16) At the same time, no mention of Indris was ever found in the 14th-to-16th-century documents, while the [Chernigov Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Russian_Chronicles "Old Russian Chronicles") used by Pyotr Tolstoy as a reference were lost.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-rummel-13) The first documented members of the Tolstoy family also lived during the 17th century, thus Pyotr Tolstoy himself is generally considered the founder of the noble house, being granted the title of [count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count") by [Peter the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great "Peter the Great").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-18)

## Life and career

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_%284x5_cropped%29.jpg/250px-Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_%284x5_cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leo_Nikolaevich_Tolstoy_poses_for_a_portrait_at_the_age_of_20_(4x5_cropped).jpg)

Tolstoy at age 20, c.1848

Tolstoy was born at [Yasnaya Polyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasnaya_Polyana "Yasnaya Polyana"), a family estate 12 kilometres (7.5 mi) southwest of [Tula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tula,_Russia "Tula, Russia"), and 200 kilometres (120 mi) south of Moscow. He was the fourth of five children of [Count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")[Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Ilyich_Tolstoy "Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy") (1794–1837), a veteran of the [Patriotic War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia "French invasion of Russia"), and Princess Mariya Tolstaya (née [Volkonskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkonsky "Volkonsky"); 1790–1830). His mother died when he was two and his father when he was nine.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) Tolstoy and his siblings were brought up by relatives.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) In 1844, he began studying law and oriental languages at [Kazan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazan_University "Kazan University"), where teachers described him as "both unable and unwilling to learn".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) Tolstoy left the university in the middle of his studies,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) returned to Yasnaya Polyana and then spent much time in Moscow, Tula and Saint Petersburg, leading a lax and leisurely lifestyle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) He began writing during this period,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) including his first novel _[Childhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood\_(Tolstoy\_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)")_, a fictitious account of his own youth, which was published in 1852.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4) In 1851, after running up heavy gambling debts, he went with his older brother to the [Caucasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus_(geographic_region) "Caucasus (geographic region)") and joined the [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Russian_Army "Imperial Russian Army"). Tolstoy served as a young artillery officer during the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War") and was in Sevastopol during the 11-month-long [siege of Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sevastopol_(1854%E2%80%9355) "Siege of Sevastopol (1854–55)") in 1854–55,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-BBCTen-20) including the [Battle of the Chernaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Chernaya "Battle of the Chernaya"). During the war he was recognised for his courage and promoted to lieutenant.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-BBCTen-20) He was appalled by the number of deaths involved in warfare,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) and left the army after the end of the Crimean War.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Britannica-4)

His experience in the army, and two trips around Europe in 1857 and 1860–61 converted Tolstoy from a dissolute and privileged society author to a non-violent and spiritual [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism"). Others who followed the same path were [Alexander Herzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Herzen "Alexander Herzen"), [Mikhail Bakunin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Bakunin "Mikhail Bakunin") and [Peter Kropotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kropotkin "Peter Kropotkin"). During his 1857 visit, Tolstoy witnessed a public execution in Paris, a traumatic experience that marked the rest of his life. In a letter to his friend [Vasily Botkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Botkin "Vasily Botkin"), Tolstoy wrote: "The truth is that the State is a conspiracy designed not only to exploit, but above all to corrupt its citizens ... Henceforth, I shall never serve any government anywhere."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-21) Tolstoy's concept of [non-violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-violence "Non-violence") or [ahimsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa "Ahimsa") was bolstered when he read a [German version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirukkural_translations_into_German "Tirukkural translations into German") of the [Tirukkural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirukkural "Tirukkural").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-PearlsOfInsp_Rajaram-22)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Walsh2018-23) He later instilled the concept in [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") through his "_[A Letter to a Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Letter\_to\_a\_Hindu "A Letter to a Hindu")_" when young Gandhi corresponded with him seeking his advice.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-Walsh2018-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-gandhi-25)

His European trip in 1860–61 shaped both his political and literary development when he met [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo"). Tolstoy read Hugo's newly finished _[Les Misérables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Mis%C3%A9rables "Les Misérables")_. The similar evocation of battle scenes in Hugo's novel and Tolstoy's _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ indicates this influence. Tolstoy's political philosophy was also influenced by a March 1861 visit to French anarchist [Pierre-Joseph Proudhon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Joseph_Proudhon "Pierre-Joseph Proudhon"), then living in exile under an assumed name in Brussels. Tolstoy reviewed Proudhon's forthcoming publication, _La Guerre et la Paix_ ("_War and Peace_" in French), and later used the title for his masterpiece. The two men also discussed education, as Tolstoy wrote in his educational notebooks: "If I recount this conversation with Proudhon, it is to show that, in my personal experience, he was the only man who understood the significance of education and of the printing press in our time."

Fired by enthusiasm, Tolstoy returned to Yasnaya Polyana and founded 13 schools for the children of Russia's peasants, who had just been [emancipated from serfdom in 1861](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_reform_of_1861 "Emancipation reform of 1861"). Tolstoy described the schools' principles in his 1862 essay "The School at Yasnaya Polyana".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-26) His educational experiments were short-lived, partly due to harassment by the [Tsarist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") secret police. However, as a direct forerunner to [A.S. Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.S._Neill "A.S. Neill")'s [Summerhill School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summerhill_School "Summerhill School"), the school at Yasnaya Polyana[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-27) can justifiably be claimed the first example of a coherent theory of [democratic education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_education "Democratic education").

## Personal life

The death of his brother Nikolay in 1860 had an impact on Tolstoy, and led him to a desire to marry.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-AuthorDataSheet-19) On 23 September 1862, Tolstoy married [Sophia Andreevna Behrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Tolstaya "Sophia Tolstaya"), who was sixteen years his junior and the daughter of a court physician. She was called Sonya, the Russian diminutive of Sofia, by her family and friends.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28) They had 13 children, eight of whom survived childhood:[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-29)

Tolstoy, on the eve of their marriage, gave her his diaries detailing his extensive sexual past and the fact that one of the serfs on his estate had borne him a son.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28) Even so, their early married life was happy and allowed Tolstoy much freedom and the support system to compose _War and Peace_ and _Anna Karenina_, with Sonya acting as his secretary, editor, and financial manager. Sonya was copying and hand-writing his epic works time after time. Tolstoy would continue editing _War and Peace_ and had to have clean final drafts to be delivered to the publisher.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-nyt-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-30)

However, their later life together has been described by [A.N. Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.N._Wilson "A.N. Wilson") as one of the unhappiest in literary history. Tolstoy's relationship with his wife deteriorated as his beliefs became increasingly radical. This saw him seeking to reject his inherited and earned wealth, including the renunciation of the copyrights on his earlier works.

When he was finishing up the last installments of _Anna Karenina_ Tolstoy was in an anguished state of mind and he began putting away guns and ropes out of fear that he would kill himself.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-31)

Some members of the Tolstoy family left Russia in the aftermath of the [1905 Russian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1905_Russian_Revolution "1905 Russian Revolution"), or after the establishment of the Soviet Union following the 1917 [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution"), and many of Leo Tolstoy's relatives and descendants today live in Sweden, Germany, the United Kingdom, France and the United States. Tolstoy's son, Count [Lev Lvovich Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev_Lvovich_Tolstoy "Lev Lvovich Tolstoy"), settled in Sweden and married a Swedish woman, and their descendants with family names including Tolstoy, [Paus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paus_family "Paus family") and Ceder still live in Sweden. The Paus branch of the family is also closely related to [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-32) Leo Tolstoy's last surviving grandchild, Countess [Tatiana Tolstoy-Paus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatiana_Tolstoy-Paus "Tatiana Tolstoy-Paus"), died in 2007 at [Herresta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herresta "Herresta") manor in Sweden, which is owned by Tolstoy's descendants.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-33) Swedish writer Daria Paus and jazz singer [Viktoria Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktoria_Tolstoy "Viktoria Tolstoy") are among Leo Tolstoy's Swedish descendants.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-34)

One of his great-great-grandsons, Vladimir Tolstoy (born 1962), has been a director of the [Yasnaya Polyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasnaya_Polyana "Yasnaya Polyana") museum since 1994 and an adviser to the [President of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Russia "President of Russia") on cultural affairs since 2012.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-36)[Ilya Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Tolstoy "Ilya Tolstoy")'s great-grandson, [Pyotr Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Olegovich_Tolstoy "Pyotr Olegovich Tolstoy"), is a well-known Russian journalist and TV presenter as well as a [State Duma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_State_Duma "7th State Duma") deputy since 2016. His cousin [Fyokla Tolstaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyokla_Tolstaya "Fyokla Tolstaya") (born Anna Tolstaya in 1971), daughter of the acclaimed Soviet [Slavist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavist "Slavist") Nikita Tolstoy ([ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%BE%D0%BB%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B9,%20%D0%9D%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B8%D1%82%D0%B0%20%D0%98%D0%BB%D1%8C%D0%B8%D1%87 "ru:Толстой, Никита Ильич")) (1923–1996), is also a Russian journalist, TV and radio host.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-37) American actress [Pati Behrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pati_Behrs "Pati Behrs") (1922–2004) was his wife's great-niece and her daughter, screenwriter [Sean Catherine Derek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Catherine_Derek "Sean Catherine Derek") (b. 1953), is her great-grandniece.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-38)

## Novels and fictional works

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy%2C_1873.jpg/250px-Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy%2C_1873.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ivan_Nikolayevich_Kramskoi_-_Portrait_of_Leo_Tolstoy,_1873.jpg)

Portrait of Leo Tolstoy by [Ivan Kramskoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Kramskoi "Ivan Kramskoi"), 1873

Tolstoy is considered one of the giants of Russian literature; his works include the novels _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ and _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina "Anna Karenina")_ and novellas such as _[Hadji Murat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadji\_Murat\_(novella) "Hadji Murat (novella)")_ and _[The Death of Ivan Ilyich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_of\_Ivan\_Ilyich "The Death of Ivan Ilyich")_. Tolstoy's earliest works, the autobiographical novels [_Childhood_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childhood_(Tolstoy_novel) "Childhood (Tolstoy novel)"), [_Boyhood_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyhood_(novel) "Boyhood (novel)"), and [_Youth_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_(Tolstoy_novel) "Youth (Tolstoy novel)") (1852–1856), tell of a rich landowner's son and his slow realization of the chasm between himself and his peasants. Though he later rejected them as sentimental, a great deal of Tolstoy's own life is revealed. They retain their relevance as accounts of the universal story of growing up. Tolstoy served as a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podporuchik "Podporuchik") in an artillery regiment during the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War"), recounted in his _[Sevastopol Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol\_Sketches "Sevastopol Sketches")_. His experiences in battle helped stir his subsequent pacifism and gave him material for realistic depiction of the horrors of war in his later work.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-39)

His fiction consistently attempts to convey realistically the Russian society in which he lived.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-40)_[The Cossacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cossacks\_(novel) "The Cossacks (novel)")_ (1863) describes the [Cossack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack") life and people through a story of a Russian aristocrat in love with a Cossack girl. _Anna Karenina_ (1877) tells parallel stories of an adulterous woman trapped by the conventions and falsities of society and of a philosophical landowner (much like Tolstoy), who works alongside the peasants in the fields and seeks to reform their lives. Tolstoy not only drew from his own life experiences but also created characters in his own image, such as Pierre Bezukhov and Prince Andrei in _War and Peace_, Levin in _Anna Karenina_ and to some extent, Prince Nekhlyudov in _Resurrection_. [Richard Pevear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Pevear_and_Larissa_Volokhonsky "Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky"), who translated many of Tolstoy's works, said of Tolstoy's signature style, "His works are full of provocation and irony, and written with broad and elaborately developed rhetorical devices."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy#cite_note-41)
